rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while reducing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in subsequent injections.

Keep the gradient fixed and raise temperature to test selectivity changes in the crowded middle cluster and nearly coeluting final pair. The short initial elution window gives ample room for later gradient flattening if needed.

Halve the gradient slope at the better-performing temperature to test whether the three critical pairs separate through increased retention and altered gradient selectivity. The last peak at 5.08 minutes leaves substantial room before the time penalty begins.

Test a small temperature reduction while retaining the successful shallower gradient. This probes whether temperature selectivity can resolve the remaining critical pair without sacrificing the other separations or exceeding 10 minutes.

Return to 60 C and slightly steepen the gradient to improve the later critical pair, whose spacing decreased with the shallower gradient. This tests whether that pair can reach full resolution while the earlier pair remains near its 1.5 threshold.

Raise the starting organic fraction by one step to adjust selectivity around the nearly resolved method. The slightly shallower slope may improve the early critical pair, while the higher starting strength may preserve separation of the later pair.

Slightly lower the ending organic fraction to flatten the gradient and improve both early critical pairs. The later pair has some resolution margin, making this a targeted test for full resolution with the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Use a slope of 0.045 organic fraction per minute, between injections 6 and 7, to balance the early and later critical pairs at full resolution. The gradient remains linear throughout the expected elution window, so the lower endpoint should not affect the last peak.

Injection 8 has reached the maximum CRF; now test a higher starting organic fraction for a shorter fully resolved separation. The accompanying shallower slope may offset compression of the early critical pairs, while injection 8 remains the established best method.

Flatten the gradient modestly at the higher starting organic fraction to recover the early critical pair while testing the remaining margin in the later pair. Injection 8 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Return to the fully resolved starting composition and test a slightly steeper slope than injection 8 to shorten elution. This probes the resolution boundary of the early critical pairs while preserving injection 8 as the maximum-score fallback.

The local slope search has bracketed the fully resolved method at 60 C. Test the low-temperature selectivity regime with a broad, fast gradient to look for a different route to full resolution in less than 7.45 minutes; injection 8 already secures the maximum CRF.

Slightly flatten the promising low-temperature gradient to test whether both critical pairs improve while keeping the last peak near seven minutes. This could yield a shorter fully resolved alternative to injection 8.

Test a higher starting organic fraction at 25 C to shorten retention and alter the balance between the two critical pairs. The previous slope change helped one pair but hurt the other, so changing the starting composition provides a distinct selectivity lever.

Continue increasing the starting organic fraction, which shortened the last run while improving both critical pairs. This tests whether the trend can produce a faster fully resolved method; injection 8 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Slightly flatten the gradient to lift the sole remaining critical pair from R 1.43 toward full resolution. This small adjustment tests whether the earlier pairs retain sufficient separation while keeping the last peak well below five minutes.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to seek an even shorter fully resolved separation. Monitor the middle pairs for selectivity loss while testing whether the slightly shallower slope preserves the late critical pair.

Slightly flatten the gradient to improve the middle critical pair, following its favorable response to flattening at phi0 0.30. This may recover full resolution while retaining a shorter elution time than injection 16.

Raise temperature one step from the fastest fully resolved method to test whether retention can be shortened without losing the modest resolution margins. Injection 18 remains the preferred fully resolved fallback if temperature selectivity is unfavorable.

Return to 25 C and combine a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to seek a shorter fully resolved separation. The shallower slope is intended to protect the middle critical pair that deteriorated when temperature or starting strength increased.

Shorten the programmed gradient while preserving injection 18's successful slope and temperature. The gradient reaches its endpoint at the outlet at 4.65 minutes, after the expected last peak at 4.14 minutes, so full resolution should be retained.

Further flatten the gradient at phi0 0.40 to test whether the middle critical pair can recover full resolution before the time advantage disappears. Injection 21 remains the shortest-programmed fully resolved fallback.

Test whether a lower starting organic fraction and shallower slope can restore the middle-pair resolution lost at 30 C. This may retain the temperature-driven time advantage while achieving full resolution; injection 21 remains the established fallback.

Steepen the gradient at 30 C to improve the early critical pair and shorten the last peak's retention. The neighboring middle pair has some resolution margin, so this tests whether both can remain above 1.5 in a faster separation.

Use the final injection to test a slightly shallower gradient around the fastest fully resolved region, seeking greater resolution margin while retaining CRF 1.000. Injection 21 remains the preferred method if shortest demonstrated elution time is the deciding criterion.
